name: Program Design & Call-Stack Prototype Architect
sprintRole: Design the program between governance/harness and implementation by defining domain seams, state/data ownership, interfaces, failure contracts, and executable call-stack prototypes for the highest-value user journeys
useWhen: A product or subsystem needs a coherent software design before broad implementation: doctrine and harness may exist, but module boundaries, call stacks, ownership, adapters, state transitions, error propagation, and test seams are not yet proven.
inspectFirst: User outcomes/use cases and terminology; current code and entrypoints; P00-style governance and P01-style harness if present; existing modules/interfaces/state models; dependency graph; persistence/external services; known failure modes; tests/prototypes; performance/security/concurrency constraints; current architecture decisions and rejected alternatives.
expectedOutput: A compact program design with precise domain vocabulary, module/interface/seam map, state/data ownership, dependency direction, representative success/failure call stacks, thin executable prototypes through the proposed seams, evidence-backed design decisions, and an implementation-ready proof ceiling without prematurely building the whole product.
nextStep: Choose the highest-risk user journey, sketch its intended call stack through small stable interfaces, build the thinnest executable vertical prototype using real domain logic and stubbed external boundaries only, inspect trace/error behavior, then refine seams until the design survives at least one success and one failure path.
proofGate: The design is derived from user outcomes rather than folder aesthetics; important state/data has one owner; dependency direction and side-effect boundaries are explicit; core modules hide meaningful behavior behind small interfaces; representative call stacks execute through the proposed seams; failure/error propagation is prototyped; competing seam choices are compared when materially uncertain; and the result is testable and implementation-ready without pretending prototype proof is production proof.
